Gorgonzola.label: pierce, grow blue

facts.v: Pasteurised whole cow's milk
Calf rennet at 28–36 °C
Lactic starters plus Penicillium spores and selected yeasts in the milk
24 h in perforated moulds (fasceruoli)
Dry salted for several days at 18–24 °C
Pierced; −1 to 7 °C, 85–100% RH; dolce 50–150 d, piccante 80–270 d

Gorgonzola.text: Gorgonzola is made from pasteurised cow's milk inoculated with Penicillium spores, then the paste is perforated during maturation so the mould can develop blue-green veins. Cold, very humid storage and a defined ripening window separate the soft, sweet dolce from the firmer, sharper piccante.

Stilton.label: needle-pierce

facts.v: Pasteurised full-cream cow's milk from Leics, Derbys, Notts
Starter plus animal or non-animal rennet
Penicillium roqueforti added to the milk and/or sprayed on curds
Cut, then next day milled to walnut-sized pieces
Cylindrical moulds, no applied pressure; turned for up to 7 d
Dry salt mixed into the milled curd
Pierced with steel needles at about 6 wk; Blue Stilton 6–12 wk
Surface sealed; forms its own slightly wrinkled coat

Stilton.text: Because the milled curd is never pressed, it settles with tiny airways between the pieces; the sealed surface keeps them closed until steel needles let air in at about six weeks and the Penicillium roqueforti starts veining from the centre. The cheese forms its own crust rather than having one applied.

Danish Blue.label: pierce, grow blue

facts.v: Danish cow's milk, standardised, homogenised and thermised/pasteurised
Rennet added after acidification
Acid starter and blue mould cultures
Moulded and drained; flat cylinder ca. 3 kg or block ca. 4 kg
Salted after draining, then pierced with needles
Minimum 5 weeks
White to light yellowish, no appreciable smear or mould growth

Danish Blue.text: Homogenising the cheese milk, a Danish practice since 1927, gives Danablu its sharp, piquant flavour and cuttable, slightly crumbly texture. Needle piercing after salting spreads the blue mould through holes and cracks while the rind stays almost clean.

sources.name: Danablu PGI amendment and single document, OJ C 151 (2012)

Cabrales.label: cave-ripen

table.v:
raw cow, sheep or goat
or a mix

facts.v: Raw whole cow's, sheep or goat milk, or a mix of two or all three
Rennet of animal origin only
Dry salt on top 12+ h, turned, other side 12+ h
Aired ~15 d, then caves at 6–10 °C, >90% RH; 2+ mo in total
Turned and cleaned on wooden shelves; wrapped in leaf-printed paper

Cabrales.text: Cabrales is finished in limestone caves of the Picos de Europa whose draughts carry Penicillium roqueforti spores off the walls onto the cheese, where they germinate and spread through the paste. The cold, saturated cave air and two to five months on wooden shelves give its strong blue veining.

sources.name: Cabrales PDO single document, OJ C 61 (2018)

Époisses.label: wash in marc

facts.v: Whole cow's milk
Predominantly lactic coagulation; rennet the only coagulant allowed
Rough cut without breaking up the curd; drained naturally
Dry salted
At least 4 weeks, washed with water containing marc de Bourgogne
Smooth, glossy, pale orange to brick red, no colourant

Époisses.text: A slow, mostly lactic set gives a fragile, moist curd that is ladled with little cutting and left to drain by itself. Repeated washing with marc de Bourgogne water during at least four weeks develops the brick-red colour and pungent aroma of the rind.

sources.name: Époisses PDO amendment summary, OJ C 280 (2007)

Munster.label: smear the rind

facts.v: Cow's milk, raw or pasteurised (farm Munster raw only)
Calf rennet on acidified curd; pH 4.5–4.9 in core at 5 d
Red smear flora, mainly Brevibacterium linens, plus yeasts
Cylindrical moulds, drained unpressed ≥15 h; 7.5–19 cm diameter
Salted after draining
21+ d (14+ d small); ≥90% RH, wet stage at 10–16 °C
2–3+ wet treatments with rubbing; ivory-orange to red-orange

Munster.text: The acidified curd is first left to deacidify, then repeatedly wetted and rubbed with water that may carry Brevibacterium linens, so red bacteria and yeasts colonise the rind. This gives the thin orange smear and pungent, slightly ammoniac smell over a sweet, melting paste.

sources.name: Munster PDO amendment and single document, OJ C 295 (2020)

Limburger.label: smear the rind

facts.v: Pasteurised cow's milk (Dutch factory studied)
Starter and rennet
Surface smear of yeasts, coryneforms incl. Brevibacterium linens
Curd set in wooden forms, cut into ~250 g blocks
Dipped in brine overnight
About 3–4 wk at ~15 °C, high humidity, rubbed a few times

Limburger.text: Limburger ripens mainly from the outside: a smear of yeasts followed by coryneform bacteria such as Brevibacterium linens grows on the surface and drives the breakdown of the paste. Rubbing closes surface openings and spreads these organisms over the whole block.

sources.name: El-Erian, Bacteriological studies on Limburger cheese (Wageningen, 1969)

Taleggio.label: wipe the rind

facts.v: Whole cow's milk, raw or pasteurised
Liquid calf rennet at 32–35 °C after lactic starters
Cut in stages to hazelnut size
Square moulds; 8–16 h stewing at 20–28 °C; 1.5–2.5 kg
Dry and/or in brine
35+ d at 1–6 °C, >80% RH, often on wooden boards
Turned and wiped with salt water only; thin, soft, natural pink

Taleggio.text: During at least 35 days in cold, humid caves or rooms the square cheeses are turned and wiped with salt water, which keeps the rind moist and removes mould hyphae. The resulting pink rind flora ripens the paste from the outside in, so it is softer under the rind than at the centre.

Herve.label: wash the rind

facts.v: Untreated or pasteurised cow's milk
Rennet; curd cut into 4 after 1.5 h
Cut to hazelnut size 15 min later, then drained
Pressed lightly between wooden planks, cut into cubes; 50–400 g
Cubes salted, then sold to ripeners
Damp cellars, washed 2–3×/wk first fortnight, then weekly
Brown, slightly rosy, from local ferments

Herve.text: The small curd cubes are washed in damp cellars, often at first and then weekly, so local smear ferments form a brown, slightly rosy rind. Ripening runs inward from that rind, leaving the paste more unctuous and mature under it than at the centre.

sources.name: Fromage de Herve PDO registration summary (eAmbrosia)

Emmentaler.label: grow eyes

table.v:
30–70 d warm room
5+ mo in total

facts.v: Raw cow's milk, never heated above 40 °C, within 24 h
Rennet; coagulation 35–45 min in copper vat
Defined lactic cultures plus propionic acid bacteria cultures
Heated to 52–54 °C in 30–60 min; moulded at 49–52 °C
Pressed up to 20 h; 80–100 cm, 75–120 kg wheels
Brine bath 20–22 °Bé for 24–72 h
Warm room 19–24 °C for 30–70 d, then cellar 11–14 °C; 5+ mo
Firm, yellow-brown; washed when moved to the cool cellar

Emmentaler.text: Weeks in the warm fermentation cellar drive the propionic acid fermentation that gives Emmentaler its regular, mostly 2–4 cm holes and its sweet, slightly tangy, mildly spicy taste. The wheels are then washed and moved to a cool cellar to mature.

Gruyère.label: smear the rind

facts.v: Raw cow's milk, delivered twice daily, stored at 12–18 °C
Rennet at about 31 °C; coagulation 30–50 min, open copper vat
Whey (Sirten) cultures, optionally RMK milk cultures
Heated to 54–59 °C
Pressed 16+ h; 55–65 cm, 25–40 kg
Brine over 20 °Bé at 12–20 °C
12–18 °C at ~92% RH; at least 5 months
Rubbed daily for 8–12 d, salt water to start smear; brownish

Gruyère.text: Instead of a warm propionic room, Gruyère goes straight into cool, humid cellars where the wheels are rubbed with salt water to grow a smear. The smear drives flavour and aroma, and holes are welcome but not required.

Comté.label: ripen in stages

facts.v: Raw whole milk of Montbéliarde or French Simmental cows
Rennet in copper vats; milk pre-ripened 40+ min before renneting
Starters, total ≤0.5% of milk volume
Heated to at most 57 °C
Pressed; 50–70 cm wheels, 35–45 kg at day 50
Dry-salted on the surface or in brine
Pre-ripening to day 21+, fermentation, then ripening; 120+ d
Smeared, rubbed with solution kept ≤13 °C; ochre yellow

Comté.text: After pre-ripening, Comté goes through a separate fermentation stage and then ripening, and its paste can show some openings up to the size of a small cherry. Long ripening with a rubbed smear rind builds fruity (hazelnut, citrus) and toasted aromas.

sources.name: Comté PDO amendment and single document (2026)

Beaufort.label: press in a hoop

facts.v: Raw whole milk of Tarine or Abondance cows, used soon after milking
Rennet from calf stomachs
Cut small, scalded and stirred
Linen cloth, wooden hoop gives concave heel; 20 h press; 20–70 kg
Brine, then surface salting
Cold cellar, at least 5 months (registration: up to 12)
Washed, firm rind

Beaufort.text: Ripening in a cold cellar keeps the paste supple and almost free of holes, unlike the eyed alpine cheeses. The wooden Beaufort hoop pressed around the cloth-wrapped curd gives the wheel its concave heel.

sources.name: Beaufort PDO amendment and single document (2025)

Appenzeller.label: rub with herbs

table.v:
Classic 3+ mo
Surchoix 4+ mo
Extra 6+ mo

facts.v: Raw cow's milk, partly skimmed
Rennet and lactic bacteria at 31 °C; about 30 min
Cut to maize-grain size; 40–42 °C when lifted from vat
Round moulds, pressed twice 15 min; 6–8 kg, ~30 cm
Brine bath about 2 days
13–14 °C, 92% RH; Classic 3+, Surchoix 4+, Extra 6+ mo
Rubbed every 2 days with secret herbal brine (Kräutersulz)

Appenzeller.text: Throughout ripening the wheels are rubbed every two days with a herbal brine, the Kräutersulz, which treats the rind as the cheese matures. Scalded only to about 40–42 °C and made in 6–8 kg wheels, it differs from the large, high-cooked Emmentaler and Gruyère.

Cheddar.label: cheddar

facts.v: Cow's milk from the farm's own herd and local farms
Starter culture and rennet
Cut and scalded at about 103–106 °F (39–41 °C)
Cheddared: slabs turned and stacked by hand, milled, pressed
Salt mixed into milled curd
At least 9 months in the area
Sealed and wrapped after pressing

Cheddar.text: Turning and stacking the curd slabs by hand (cheddaring) comes before milling, salting and mechanical pressing. At least nine months of natural maturing gives a nutty, full, rounded flavour with a hint of sharpness.

sources.name: West Country Farmhouse Cheddar PDO summary (eAmbrosia)

Red Leicester.label: colour with annatto

facts.v: Cow's milk
Cheddared before pressing
Usually 4–9 months; farmhouse wheels clothbound
Reddish-orange, coloured with annatto since the 18th century

Red Leicester.text: Annatto added during making turns the paste deep orange. Traditional wheels are firm, dry and friable, while block cheeses from creameries are moister and creamier.

Double Gloucester.label: age longer

facts.v: Full-fat cow's milk, traditionally from Gloucester cattle
Natural rind; paste pale to deep red-orange

Double Gloucester.text: Double Gloucester is made with full-fat milk, whereas Single Gloucester is often made from part-skimmed milk. It is aged longer than Single, which gives a stronger, more savoury flavour.

sources.name: Slow Food UK: Artisan Single and Double Gloucester
Single Gloucester PDO summary (eAmbrosia), for contrast

Dunlop.label: scald the rind

facts.v: Whole Ayrshire cow's milk, raw or pasteurised (72 °C, 15 s)
Lactic starter, ripened 1 h at 30 °C; rennet 40–50 min
Cut to ¼ in cubes, stirred at 38 °C for 60–90 min
Slabs cut and turned, pegmilled at 0.55–0.65% acidity; pressed overnight
Sea salt mixed into milled curd, ~1 kg per 100 gal milk
6–18 months, most popular 10–12 months
Scalded in hot water, wrapped in scalded cloth; thin golden rind

Dunlop.text: The small fat globules of Ayrshire milk let more fat stay in the curd, giving a moist, smooth, close texture that becomes slightly springy. Scalding the pressed cheese and binding it in hot cloth forms its thin golden rind.

Cheese curds.label: salt the curd

facts.v: Made as for Cheddar but kept as separate milled pieces
Salted right away; higher moisture than Cheddar
None; squeak is best fresh

Cheese curds.text: Curds are taken from the Cheddar process after milling and salted instead of being pressed into a block. While fresh, their casein network is tightly linked by calcium phosphate, so it rebounds against the teeth and squeaks; acid and rennet break those links as they age.

sources.name: Cheese Market News: Cheese of the Month, cheese curds (2017), citing CDR

Gouda.label: wash the curd

facts.v: Dutch cow's milk, pasteurised ≥72 °C for 15 s
Rennet at about 30 °C
Non-GM lactic-acid and aroma-forming cultures
Separated from whey and washed to set moisture and pH
Pressed in moulds; flattened cylinder or block, 2.5–20 kg
Immersed in brine bath
Natural rind, at least 28 d at a minimum of 12 °C, no foil

Gouda.text: Washing the curd after the whey is drawn off is how the maker sets the moisture and pH of the cheese before it is pressed and brined. It is slightly soft to pliable at four weeks and becomes firmer as it matures for up to more than a year.

Edam.label: part-skim

facts.v: Cow's milk, partially skimmed and pasteurised
Calf rennet
Mesophilic L or LD starters (Lactococcus lactis, Leuconostoc)
Noord-Hollandse Edammer: sphere with flat ends, 1.7–1.9 kg
Brine bath for a few days
At least 28 d (21 d for Baby Edam)

Edam.text: Edam is made from partially skimmed milk, so it has 40–44% fat in dry matter against 48–52% for Gouda Holland. The Noord-Hollandse Edammer is moulded as a small sphere with flat top and bottom.

sources.name: Gouda Holland PGI, Regulation (EU) No 1122/2010 (fat comparison)

Colby.label: cool the curd

facts.v: Cooled by adding water while stirring so the pieces don't mat
Drained, salted, stirred, pressed into forms
If made from raw milk, cured 60+ d at ≥35 °F (1.7 °C)

Colby.text: Adding water to cool the stirred curd stops the pieces from matting together into slabs, the step that defines cheddaring. The pieces are then drained, salted and pressed, giving a cheese with up to 40% moisture.

sources.name: 21 CFR 133.118 Colby cheese (US standard of identity)

Leyden.label: add cumin

facts.v: Raw semi-skimmed cow's milk, cooled to ≤10 °C
Rennet for half an hour at 29–30 °C
Chopped; curds and whey heated by adding hot water
Cumin ~75 g/100 L milk; plain-curd 'white bottoms'; 2-stage press
Brine at 20 °Bé for 5–6 days
Cheeses ≥3 kg kept 13+ d at ≥12 °C
Coloured red with annatto; stamped with crossed keys of Leiden

Leyden.text: Leyden is made from partly skimmed milk with cumin seed worked into the curd, while plain curd on the flat faces keeps the seeds out of the rind. The rind is coloured red with annatto and stamped with Leiden's crossed keys.

Maasdam.label: grow eyes

facts.v: Cow's milk, often centrifuged to remove spores (spore-sensitive type)
Lactococcus starter, Lb. helveticus, Propionibacterium (PAB)
Curd grains washed with water to lower lactose and final pH
Curd drained and pre-pressed under whey, giving a closed, round-eyed body
Warm-room stage in which propionic bacteria multiply and make eyes

Maasdam.text: Maasdam is a washed-curd Dutch cheese to which propionic acid bacteria are added; during a warm-room stage they multiply and ferment lactate to CO2, propionate and acetate, giving large round eyes and a sweet, nutty taste. Its low salt, high moisture and warm ripening make it prone to butyric spoilage, so the milk is often centrifuged to remove spores.

sources.name: Tetra Pak Dairy Processing Handbook, ch. Cheese
Lamichhane et al., J. Dairy Sci. 101:5738 (2018)

Casu marzu.label: lure the fly

facts.v: Whole sheep's milk of the Sarda breed, made into pecorino
Rennet (pecorino make)
Larvae of the cheese fly Piophila casei inside the wheel
Lightly pressed cylinders, mostly 2–4 kg
Brining shortened so salt does not deter the fly
Few turnings; small holes with drops of oil in rind; late spring–autumn
A lid (su tappu) is cut in one face to check and serve the creamy paste

Casu marzu.text: Pecorino is deliberately made attractive to the cheese fly: it is lightly pressed, briefly brined and its rind pierced and oiled, so that Piophila casei lays its eggs inside. The larvae break down the paste, which turns soft to spreadably creamy with a strong, penetrating, piquant taste.

Casgiu merzu.label: lure the fly

facts.v: Sheep's or goat's milk, as a whole tomme
Larvae of the cheese fly Piophila casei
Tomme matured in an airy place open to flies, which lay eggs on it
Inside becomes a very soft paste riddled with larval galleries

Casgiu merzu.text: A whole Corsican sheep's- or goat's-milk tomme is left where cheese flies can lay their eggs; the larvae feeding inside break the paste down into a very soft, tunnelled mass that weeps a liquid called 'lagrima'.

Marcetto.label: let larvae soften

facts.v: Pecorino of whole raw sheep's milk
Rennet, liquid or powder diluted in water
Piophila casei larvae colonise young or cracked wheels
Once the whole wheel is creamy, paste scraped into terracotta/glass jars
Cool room 10–14 °C, 85–90% RH; larvae break down the proteins

Marcetto.text: Pecorino wheels that are still moist with whey or have cracked rinds are colonised by cheese-fly larvae, whose activity breaks down the proteins until the whole wheel turns creamy and very piquant. The paste is then scraped out and kept refrigerated in terracotta or glass jars as a spreadable cream.

sources.name: Regione Abruzzo PAT sheet 'Cacio marcetto' (via ONAF)

Mimolette.label: mite-ripen

facts.v: Pasteurised cow's milk
Animal rennet 0.04–0.25 mL/L; annatto (rocou) ≤0.35 mL/L for orange
Lactic starters; cheese mites on the rind during ripening
Cut curd, grains washed (≤30% water) and reheated in the vat
Pressed; sphere flattened at the poles, 2–4 kg
Saturated brine, 48–72 h at 10–15 °C
8–16 °C, 80–95% RH; vieille ≥13 mo, extra-vieille ≥18 mo; turned, brushed
Dry, hard, 0.5–1 cm thick, mite-covered, not waxed

Mimolette.text: Mimolette is a washed-curd pressed cheese coloured with annatto and shaped into a ball; during a long cave ripening the rind is colonised by cheese mites and regularly brushed and turned, giving a dry, hard, pitted crust. Long ageing concentrates its aroma and hardens the paste.

sources.name: Label Rouge LA 26/89 'Mimolette vieille et extra-vieille' (INAO, 2014)
Shimano et al., Exp. Appl. Acarol. (2022), JST summary

Milbenkäse.label: ripen with mites

facts.v: Dried lean quark (Magerquark) of cow's, goat's or sheep's milk
Cheese mites Tyrolichus casei
Wooden boxes with mites fed rye flour; about 3–6 months
Turns amber at best ripeness

Milbenkäse.text: Small shapes of dried lean quark are kept in boxes with cheese mites, which are fed rye flour so they nibble only the surface; their activity and secretions ripen the cheese, giving a sharp, slightly bitter taste and a lemony note from the mite compound neral.

sources.name: Slow Food Deutschland, Ark of Taste: Würchwitzer Milbenkäse
Shimano et al., Exp. Appl. Acarol. (2022), JST summary

American cheese.label: melt

facts.v: Cheddar, washed-curd, colby or granular cheese, ground and mixed
Heated ≥150 °F (66 °C) for ≥30 s with ≤3% emulsifying salts (citrates, phosphates)
None after melting; moisture ≤40%, fat in solids ≥47%, pH ≥5.3

American cheese.text: Under the US standard, 'pasteurized process American cheese' is made by grinding cheddar-family cheeses and heating them with emulsifying salts into a smooth, homogeneous plastic mass. The salts bind calcium so the proteins re-emulsify the fat, which is why it melts smoothly without separating.

Cancoillotte.label: melt

facts.v: Skimmed cow's milk
Inoculated and coagulated at a controlled temperature
Drained by pressing into metton loaves, then crumbled
Metton heated to ~90 °C with water, salt, melting salts, a little butter
Metton matured at controlled temperature, stirred, until hard grains

Cancoillotte.text: Cancoillotte starts from metton, a skim-milk curd pressed and then ripened into hard, yellowish grains; melting it at about 90 °C with water and salt turns it into a runny, low-fat spread whose texture depends on how much water is added.

Requeijão cremoso.label: melt with cream

facts.v: Milk or reconstituted milk
Acid and/or enzymatic (rennet) coagulation
Curd drained of whey and washed
Melted with added cream, butter or milkfat; citrate/phosphate salts allowed
None; spreadable, fat in dry matter ≥55%, moisture ≤65%

Requeijão cremoso.text: Requeijão cremoso is made by melting a drained, washed milk curd together with cream or butter, which must be added in the 'cremoso' type, giving a smooth, spreadable, mildly acidic product sold in cups.

Plavleny syrok.label: melt

facts.v: Rennet cheeses, tvorog (quark), butter and other dairy raw materials
Melted at 75–95 °C with citrate/phosphate melting salts; sliceable or pasty
None; smoked 'sausage' type smoked about 3 h at 50–60 °C

Plavleny syrok.text: Soviet and Russian processed cheese is made by melting rennet cheeses with tvorog, butter and melting salts at 75–95 °C into a homogeneous mass, sold as dense sliceable blocks such as the 'Druzhba' foil-wrapped bar or as soft spreadable pastes.

Velveeta.label: emulsify

facts.v: Milk, whey, milk protein concentrate, milkfat, canola oil, cheese culture
Emulsified with sodium phosphate and sodium citrate; soft loaf

Velveeta.text: Velveeta is built from milk, whey and milk protein concentrate with emulsifying phosphates and citrates rather than mainly from ripened cheese, which gives its soft, velvety melt. Because milk protein concentrate is not a permitted ingredient under the US process-cheese standards, it is labelled a 'pasteurized prepared cheese product'.

sources.name: Farm and Dairy (2002), FDA warns Kraft about MPCs

Halloumi.label: cook in whey

facts.v: Sheep's/goat's milk, cow's allowed but always less; pasteurised or >65 °C
Rennet (not from pigs)
Curd pieces heated in whey above 90 °C for at least 30 min
Folded into rectangles or half-moons with Cypriot mint; 150–350 g
Salt ≤3% fresh; mature type kept ≥40 d in salted whey (≤6% salt)

Halloumi.text: Cooking the curd in whey above 90 °C sets the protein so firmly that halloumi does not melt and can be grilled or fried; it is then folded with Cypriot mint leaves, giving its characteristic shape.

Leipäjuusto.label: bake

facts.v: Pasteurised Finnish cow's, goat's or reindeer milk (Kainuu)
Rennet, with salt added to the milk
Coagulum cut and whey drained
Pressed into a flat round or rectangular sheet 0.5–3 cm thick
None; baked on both sides in oven, grill or by open fire; eaten at once
Black-brown spotted baked surface; squeaky, firm white inside

Leipäjuusto.text: A fresh rennet curd is spread into a thin sheet and baked on both sides until dark-spotted; the heat firms the squeaky curd and browns its surface, and the cheese is ready to eat straight after baking.

Queso para freír.label: fry

facts.v: Cow's milk
None; sold fresh, firm and salty

Queso para freír.text: Queso para freír is a firm, salty fresh white cheese from the Dominican Republic and Puerto Rico that softens but keeps its shape when fried, turning crisp and golden outside and soft inside.

sources.name: Tropical Cheese, Queso de Freír product page

Mozzarella di bufala.label: stretch

facts.v: Whole fresh buffalo milk, raw/thermised/pasteurised, ≤60 h after milking
Liquid calf rennet at 34–38 °C
Natural whey starter from previous buffalo-milk batches
Broken to walnut size (3–6 cm), soured under whey ~5 h
Stretched with boiling water, torn off by hand, 10–800 g (plaits ≤3 kg)
Brine, typically 10–18%
None; kept in its slightly acid, salted liquid

Mozzarella di bufala.text: Buffalo-milk curd soured with natural whey starter until it can stretch is spun in boiling water and torn into balls, giving thin overlapping layers that ooze a milky liquid; it is not ripened but sold fresh in its liquid.

sources.name: ONAF technical sheet, Mozzarella di Bufala Campana DOP

Provolone.label: stretch

table.v:
dolce up to 2–3 mo
piccante 3+ mo
stagionato 8+ mo

facts.v: Whole cow's milk; ≤6 kg pasteurised (72 °C 15 s), larger thermised ≤55 °C
36–39 °C; calf rennet (dolce) or kid/lamb rennet paste (piccante)
Acidified whey starter from the previous make
Cooked in two steps to about 51 °C; soured 6–8 h at 20 °C
Stretched in water at 80–85 °C; 0.5 kg to over 100 kg
Brine 12–25 days by size
Dolce ≤2–3 mo; piccante >3 mo; stagionato >8 mo; 15–16 °C; may be smoked

Provolone.text: Provolone Valpadana is a semi-cooked pasta filata of cow's milk that is moulded into shapes from half a kilo to over 100 kg and ripened; the sharp 'piccante' type gets its spicy taste from kid or lamb rennet paste and months of ageing.

sources.name: ONAF technical sheet, Provolone Valpadana DOP

Provoleta.label: spin the curd

facts.v: Spun (hilado) curd, provolone-style
Discs about 10–15 cm across and 1–1.5 cm thick

Provoleta.text: Provoleta is an Argentine provolone-type spun-curd cheese sold in small thick discs; the spun curd is dense enough to hold its shape when grilled whole at an asado.

Caciocavallo.label: stretch, hang

facts.v: Cow's milk, raw or thermised (58 °C, 30 s); ≤4 milkings over 2 days
36–38 °C, calf or kid rennet paste
Natural whey starter permitted
Broken to hazelnut size, soured until it can be stretched
Stretched in hot water, closed at 80–85 °C; oval or cone, 1–2.5 kg
Brine for at least 6 h, by weight
Tied in pairs and hung on poles; at least 30 days
Thin, smooth, straw-yellow, darkening with age

Caciocavallo.text: Caciocavallo Silano is a cow's-milk pasta filata moulded by hand into a closed, smooth pear or oval, then tied in pairs and hung over poles to ripen; it firms from elastic to flaky and develops a straw-yellow rind.

sources.name: ONAF technical sheet, Caciocavallo Silano DOP

Kashkaval.label: scald in brine

facts.v: Sheep's (Balkan), cow's (Vitosha) or mixed (Preslav); 60–63 °C for 20 s
Starter and rennet; coagulation 30–40 min
Pea-size, heated to 38–39 °C; cheddared 2–3 h at 35–37 °C
Sliced curd scalded 3–4 min at 72–74 °C in hot brine (5–6% salt), kneaded
About 60 days

Kashkaval.text: Kashkaval curd is cheddared until plastic, then sliced and scalded in hot salted water rather than plain water, kneaded and moulded into wheels; the brine scald salts the paste as it is stretched.

sources.name: Tetra Pak Dairy Processing Handbook, ch. Cheese

Feta.label: brine

facts.v: Sheep's milk, or with up to 30% goat's milk
Curd drained naturally in moulds
Surface dry-salted, then packed in brine of 7% NaCl
~15 d at 18 °C, ≥85% RH, then 2–4 °C; at least 2 months in total

Feta.text: Feta is drained, dry-salted and then ripened in 7% brine in barrels or tins, first briefly warm and then cold for at least two months, which keeps it white, rindless and salty with a firm, crumbly texture.

sources.name: Feta PDO registration file (Greek MD 313025/1994), eAmbrosia

Viili.text: Slime-forming Lc. lactis subsp. cremoris produce an exopolysaccharide network that binds casein into viili's stretchy, adhesive gel, while diacetylactis strains and Leuconostoc add aroma. Unhomogenised cream rises and the mould Geotrichum candidum grows a velvety skin on it.

Toba et al. 1990, Int J Food Microbiol (viili texture)

Tätmjölk.label: ferment with leaves

facts.v: Freshly milked, still-warm milk
Ropy Lc. lactis subsp. cremoris, traditionally from Pinguicula vulgaris leaves
Ropy, cohesive

Tätmjölk.text: Traditionally, warm milk was poured over fresh butterwort leaves, whose surface carries Lactococcus with exopolysaccharide genes. These seed the ropy fermentation that thickens the milk.

sources.name: Porcellato et al. 2016, J Dairy Sci (tettemelk, Pinguicula)

Varenets.label: ferment

facts.v: Cow's milk, sterilised or heat-treated at 97 ± 2 °C
Thermophilic lactic streptococci only
Smooth, set or stirred; no gas; milk-white to light cream colour

Varenets.text: Varenets is made from long-heated milk soured with thermophilic streptococci only, so it tastes clean and lactic with a distinct cooked-milk note. Traditionally it was baked milk set with smetana.

Bioghurt.label: ferment mildly

facts.v: Cow's milk, usually heated above 85 °C for some minutes
S. thermophilus with lactobacilli other than L. bulgaricus ('Joghurt mild')
Mild, only slightly sour

Bioghurt.text: Leaving out L. bulgaricus and using gentler-acidifying lactobacilli gives a yoghurt that is only mildly sour. Bioghurt was introduced in the 1950s as a German sour-milk speciality.

sources.name: Austrian Food Codex B32, Milch und Milchprodukte (2018)
'Über die neue Sauermilch-Spezialität Bioghurt' (1956), Fette Seifen

Actimel.label: ferment with probiotic

table.v:
Streptococcus thermophilus
Lactobacillus bulgaricus
Lactobacillus casei DN-114 001

facts.v: S. thermophilus, L. bulgaricus, L. casei DN-114 001, each ~10⁸ cfu/g
Drinkable fermented milk

Actimel.text: Actimel is milk fermented by the two yoghurt bacteria plus Danone's L. casei strain DN-114 001, which survives at about 10⁸ cfu per gram.

sources.name: Agarwal & Bhasin 2002, Eur J Clin Nutr (Actimel)
Marcos et al. 2004, Eur J Nutr (Actimel)

Yakult.label: ferment

facts.v: Skim milk powder, sugar, dextrose in water; heated >100 °C (HTST)
Single strain Lacticaseibacillus paracasei Shirota
Homogenised, blended with sugar syrup and flavour, diluted with water
Thin, sweet; 6.5 billion LcS per 65 mL bottle

Yakult.text: A single strain, L. paracasei Shirota, slowly sours a heat-treated sweetened skim-milk base into a concentrate. This is homogenised, mixed with syrup and diluted into a thin, sweet drink.

Acidophilus milk.label: ferment sterilised milk

facts.v: Skim milk sterilised at 121 °C, 13–15 min
Lactobacillus acidophilus (single species)
37 ± 1 °C, about 36 h
Min. 0.6% titratable acidity (Codex)
Cooled to 10–15 °C, stirred creamy, bottled

Acidophilus milk.text: Milk is sterilised so that only L. acidophilus grows, then held near body temperature until it forms a solid coagulum. The result is tangy and thickened.

sources.name: Austrian Food Codex B32, Milch und Milchprodukte (2018)

Dahi.label: ferment

table.v:
Lactococcus lactis
Lactococcus cremoris
Lactococcus diacetylactis
Leuconostoc

facts.v: Cow or buffalo; boiled traditionally, 80–85 °C industrially
Lc. lactis, Lc. cremoris, Lc. diacetylactis, Leuconostoc; household backslopped
22 °C for 12–14 h or 37 °C for 5–8 h
stopped at pH 4.4–4.5
cooled to 3–4 °C to set

Dahi.text: Mesophilic lactococci sour boiled milk into a soft set curd; diacetyl-forming Lc. diacetylactis and Leuconostoc give mild dahi its buttery note, while added thermophiles make a sourer dahi. Household dahi is backslopped from the previous batch, so its flora varies, with Lactobacillus and Streptococcus often dominant.

sources.name: Rasane et al., J. Pure Appl. Microbiol. (2017)
Dahi 16S metagenomics, J. Food Sci. Technol. (2025)

Tarag.label: ferment

table.v:
Lactobacillus delbrueckii
Lactobacillus helveticus
Lactococcus lactis
Galactomyces yeasts

facts.v: Cow, goat or yak
wild; L. delbrueckii dominant, L. helveticus, Lc. lactis; Galactomyces yeasts

Tarag.text: Tarag is a spontaneously fermented Mongolian milk in which Lactobacillus dominates (L. delbrueckii in pyrosequencing, L. helveticus and Lc. lactis among isolates), alongside yeasts such as Galactomyces. Its flora varies with region and with the animal the milk comes from.

sources.name: Oki et al., Biosci. Microbiota Food Health (2014)
Tarag bacterial/fungal diversity, J. Dairy Sci. (2014)

Matsoni.label: ferment

table.v:
Streptococcus thermophilus
Lactobacillus bulgaricus
Lactobacillus rhamnosus
yeasts

facts.v: Cow, also sheep, goat or buffalo
S. thermophilus + L. delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus; L. rhamnosus; yeasts

Matsoni.text: Matsoni, from Georgia and Armenia, is soured mainly by thermophilic S. thermophilus and L. delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus, the same pair as yoghurt, with strains carried from batch to batch. Yeasts such as Kluyveromyces marxianus vary by region and milk type.

sources.name: Matsoni LAB microbiota, Anim. Sci. J. (2007)

Labneh.label: salt, strain

facts.v: L. bulgaricus + S. thermophilus
1.2–2.5 % lactic acid; hard types about pH 4.3
salted to ~1.5 %, strained in cheesecloth overnight; industrially centrifuged or UF
spreadable; hard types 45–50 % moisture

Labneh.text: Labneh is yoghurt that has been salted and then drained of whey in cloth, which concentrates the protein into a thick, tangy spread. Codex lists it as a concentrated fermented milk, with at least 5.6 % protein.

sources.name: Codex Standard for Fermented Milks CXS 243-2003

Chakka.label: strain

facts.v: Often skim milk; heated near boiling, cooled to 30–35 °C
Lc. lactis subsp. lactis, cremoris and diacetylactis/Leuconostoc
30–35 °C, 5–7 h (traditional); ~8 h industrially
0.8–1 % lactic acid at end of setting
hung in muslin overnight, 10–12 h; or basket centrifuge / quarg separator

Chakka.text: Chakka is dahi, soured by mesophilic lactococci, that has been hung in muslin until most of the whey has run off, leaving a semi-solid mass. Chakka is the base for sweetened shrikhand.

sources.name: Rasane et al., J. Pure Appl. Microbiol. (2017)

Suzma.label: strain

facts.v: katyk (yoghurt) hung in a cloth bag to drain the whey; ~40 % yield by weight
thick, clay-like

Suzma.text: Suzma is Central Asian katyk (yoghurt) strained in cloth until thick; dried, it becomes kurut.

Doogh.label: dilute, salt

facts.v: yoghurt starter: L. delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus + S. thermophilus
~40 % yoghurt diluted with water, ~0.7 % salt; flavoured or carbonated variants
thin drink; prone to serum separation

Doogh.text: Doogh is Iranian yoghurt diluted with water and salted, sometimes flavoured with herbs or carbonated. Codex calls this a drink based on fermented milk, with at least 40 % fermented milk.

sources.name: Low-fat doogh study, Food Sci. Nutr. (2023)
Codex Standard for Fermented Milks CXS 243-2003

Tan.label: dilute, salt

facts.v: yoghurt mixed with water and salt

Tan.text: Tan is the Armenian drink of yoghurt (matsun) thinned with water and salted, close to ayran.

sources.name: Codex Standard for Fermented Milks CXS 243-2003

Mastaw.label: dilute, salt

facts.v: yoghurt mixed with water and salt

Mastaw.text: Mastaw (Kurdish mast 'yoghurt' + aw 'water') is yoghurt diluted with water and salted, the Kurdish counterpart of ayran.

sources.name: Codex Standard for Fermented Milks CXS 243-2003

Salted lassi.label: break, salt, spice

facts.v: 85 °C for 30 min or 91 °C for 2.5–5 min (industrial lassi)
inoculated at 31 °C, fermented at 22 °C to pH 4.5 (industrial)
curd broken; salt and spices (cumin) added after fermentation

Salted lassi.text: Lassi is set dahi broken up into a drink. The salted Punjabi and western Indian style adds salt and cumin after fermentation instead of sugar.

sources.name: Indian lassi review, Probiotics Antimicrob. Proteins (2026)
Rasane et al., J. Pure Appl. Microbiol. (2017)

Kashk.label: churn, boil, dry

facts.v: boiled 15–20 min, cooled to ~43 °C
1–2 % of previous day's yoghurt; industrial: S. thermophilus + L. bulgaricus
~43 °C, 3–4 h (traditional); 6–7 h industrially
churned 45–60 min, defatted; boiled 25–30 min; strained 24–48 h; salted
20–50 g balls sun-dried 1–2 wk; hard, high protein

Kashk.text: In Iran, yoghurt is churned with water to remove the butter. The defatted drink is boiled, drained in linen bags, salted, shaped and sun-dried into hard, protein-rich kashk, which is later ground and rehydrated as liquid kashk.

sources.name: Say, Soltani & Güzeler, Pamukkale Univ. J. Eng. Sci. (2015)

Qurut.label: drain, dry

facts.v: sheep, goat, cow; also mare or camel in Kazakhstan
~2 % previous day's yoghurt (Turkish kurut); K. marxianus isolated
5–8 h (Turkish kurut)
drained in linen ~1 d (or boiled down); 1–3 % salt; 40–60 g balls sun-dried 1–2 wk
hard, keeps for years

Qurut.text: Yoghurt or soured milk is drained (in Kazakhstan, first cooked down), then salted, rolled into balls and dried in sun and air. The low water content lets qurut keep for years.

sources.name: Tuganbay et al., Mol. Nutr. Food Res. (2026)
Say, Soltani & Güzeler, Pamukkale Univ. J. Eng. Sci. (2015)

Chortan.label: heat, dry

facts.v: diluted yoghurt (tan) heated, strained and dried

Chortan.text: Chortan ('dry tan') is the Armenian dried product made by heating and straining diluted yoghurt and drying the curd, the Armenian counterpart of kashk and qurut.

sources.name: Chortan fermentation study, Int. J. Food Sci. Technol. (2020)

Aaruul.label: press, dry

facts.v: cow, yak, goat or camel; mare's milk does not curd
traditionally soured milk (tarag); study used S. thermophilus + L. delbrueckii
43 °C, 4 h (study recipe)
curd drained in cloth, pressed to ~60 % moisture, cut, sun-dried 4–5 d
hard dried curd, ≤20 % moisture

Aaruul.text: Mongolian aaruul is the curd of soured or yoghurt-fermented milk, drained in cloth, pressed, cut and dried in sun and air on the yurt roof. It becomes a hard snack that keeps through winter.

sources.name: Jargalsaikhan & Dorjsuren, Mong. J. Agric. Sci. (2024)

Choormog.label: ferment camel milk

facts.v: raw camel milk, filtered, not heated
backslopped; L. kefiranofaciens dominant; also L. plantarum; yeasts
sour and alcoholic

Choormog.text: Mongolian khoormog is raw camel milk soured with leftover product. Lactobacillus dominates, chiefly L. kefiranofaciens, and yeasts give the drink a sour, slightly alcoholic taste.

sources.name: Guo et al., Food Sci. Nutr. (2021)
Oki et al., Biosci. Microbiota Food Health (2014)

Shubat.label: ferment camel milk

table.v:
Lactobacillus helveticus
Lactobacillus delbrueckii
Kluyveromyces marxianus
Kluyveromyces unispora

facts.v: raw camel milk; modern: pasteurised 63–90 °C
backslopped; L. helveticus, L. delbrueckii; yeasts K. marxianus, K. unispora
1–2 d in skin or wood (trad.); modern 20–25 °C, 3–4 h + 10–20 h
ripened 10–12 h cold; keeps 5–6 d at 5–10 °C

Shubat.text: Kazakh shubat is camel milk backslopped with old shubat. Lactobacilli such as L. helveticus make the acid, and yeasts, chiefly lactose-fermenting K. marxianus, add a little alcohol.

Gariss.label: ferment in skin bags

table.v:
Streptococcus infantarius
Lactobacillus fermentum
Kluyveromyces marxianus
Issatchenkia orientalis

facts.v: raw camel milk, no heat treatment
S. infantarius subsp. infantarius, L. fermentum; K. marxianus, I. orientalis
ambient, up to 72–96 h, in skin bags
agitated during nomadic transport

Gariss.text: Sudanese gariss ferments in large skin bags that keep a stock of soured product, shaken as the nomads travel. Streptococcus infantarius and L. fermentum make the acid, and Kluyveromyces marxianus yeasts make some alcohol.

sources.name: Abdelgadir et al., Int. J. Food Microbiol. (2008)

Suusac.label: ferment in smoked gourd

facts.v: raw camel milk milked into an Acacia-smoked gourd
wild; Lactobacillus, Lactococcus, Leuconostoc; Candida, Geotrichum yeasts
ambient, 48–96 h
fatty top layer removed; keeps ~1 wk at 26–29 °C

Suusac.text: Kenyan and Somali suusac is raw camel milk left to sour in gourds smoked with acacia twigs. The smoke flavours and colours it, while wild lactic acid bacteria and yeasts make the acid.

sources.name: Jans et al., Int. J. Food Microbiol. (2013)

Dhanaan.label: ferment in smoked can

facts.v: raw camel milk in a container smoked with Olea africana
spontaneous/backslopped; Streptococcus, Lactococcus, Weissella
ambient 25–35 °C, 12–24 h or 48–72 h
pH 4.18; 1.8 % titratable acidity
white, thin, sour

Dhanaan.text: Ethiopian Somali dhanaan is raw camel milk soured in a smoked, cloth-wrapped container. Streptococcus, Lactococcus and Weissella dominate the lactic flora, which gives a thin, sour drink, often topped up with fresh milk.

sources.name: Ethiopian fermented milk review, Food Sci. Nutr. (2024)

facts.v: fat globules average about 3.5 µm across
below 1 µm; fat surface area grows about 4–6 fold
first stage 100–250 bar (e.g. 200 bar), second stage back-pressure about 30 bar
55–80 °C; below 40 °C the fat is broken up poorly

homogenised.text: Warm milk is pumped at high pressure through a narrow gap, which tears the fat globules into droplets under 1 µm. Droplets that small stay suspended, so no cream layer forms on top.

sources.name: Tetra Pak Dairy Processing Handbook: Homogenizers

facts.v: at least 72 °C for 15 s, or at least 63 °C for 30 min
161 °F (72 °C) for 15 s, or 145 °F (63 °C) for 30 min
usually 72–75 °C for 15–20 s for homogenised milk
alkaline phosphatase test must come out negative
7–10 d unopened at 5–7 °C

pasteurised.text: A short heat to 72 °C kills the disease-causing bacteria but not all spoilage organisms, so the milk must stay chilled and keeps for about a week. The destroyed milk enzyme alkaline phosphatase is the test that proves it was heated enough.

sources.name: Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, Annex III, Section IX, Ch. II
Tetra Pak Dairy Processing Handbook: Pasteurized and ESL dairy products

facts.v: 85–127 °C for 1–4 s; one optimised option is 130 °C for 1 s
or 1.4 µm microfilter removes up to 99.99 % of bacteria and spores, then 72 °C for 15–20 s
12–21 d chilled; 2–4 wk with 1.4 µm filter or HHT
chilled chain should stay at or below 8 °C

esl.text: ESL milk gets either a hotter heat than pasteurisation or a pass through a microfilter that holds back bacteria and spores. It still needs the fridge, but keeps for two to three weeks instead of one.

sources.name: Tetra Pak Dairy Processing Handbook: Pasteurized and ESL dairy products
Verbraucherzentrale Niedersachsen: Milch – was verrät das Etikett?

facts.v: not less than 135 °C with a suitable holding time, in continuous flow
typically 137–142 °C for 4–6 s
ultra-pasteurized: at least 138 °C for at least 2 s
stable after 15 d at 30 °C or 7 d at 55 °C in closed packs
at least 12 wk; 3–9 months depending on market

uht.text: Milk flows through a heater to at least 135 °C for a few seconds, which leaves no germs or spores that could grow, and is then filled aseptically. Unopened it keeps for months without refrigeration.

sources.name: Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, Annex III, Section IX, Ch. II
Tetra Pak Dairy Processing Handbook: Long-life dairy products

facts.v: batch, 110–125 °C for 3–40 min
hydrostatic, 115–125 °C for 3–30 min
112–120 °C for 20–40 min; 12 months shelf life
large vitamin losses

sterilised.text: The milk is filled and sealed first, then the whole bottle is heated for many minutes. That long heat makes it keep for about a year, but destroys more of the vitamins.

sources.name: Tetra Pak Dairy Processing Handbook: Long-life dairy products
Verbraucherzentrale Niedersachsen: Milch – was verrät das Etikett?

Jameed.label: strain, dry

facts.v: Mostly sheep's milk, weakly heated, soured by its own flora, churned
Heated buttermilk strained in cloth bags, kneaded with salt, shaped into balls
Sun-dried to about 20 % moisture, about 15 days
Market samples: pH about 3.7; salt 11.7 %; 62–92 % solids
Stone-hard balls that keep up to two years

Jameed.text: Jameed is the curd of churned sour yoghurt, strained, heavily salted and dried in the sun. Low moisture, low pH and high salt together let it keep for up to two years.

sources.name: Hamad et al., J. Food Technology Research 3(2) (2016)
